flawed_step: The step from 'a stable matching exists' (Gale–Shapley) to 'the stable matching is unique' cannot be justified. The matching found when men propose can differ from the one found when women propose.
counterexample: n=2. Preferences: m1: w1>w2; m2: w2>w1; w1: m2>m1; w2: m1>m2. Matching A = {m1-w1, m2-w2}: each man has his first choice, so no man belongs to a blocking pair and A is stable. Matching B = {m1-w2, m2-w1}: each woman has her first choice (w1 has m2, w2 has m1), so no woman belongs to a blocking pair and B is stable. A and B are different, so there are two stable matchings.
assessment_summary: False. A stable matching always exists but need not be unique. The 2x2 instance with opposite preferences on the two sides has two stable matchings: the one best for the men and the one best for the women.
